content: Oxytocin, also known as Oxt, is a peptide hormone and neuropeptide. It is synthesized in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus and released by the posterior pituitary gland. This hormone plays a critical role in social bonding, sexual reproduction, childbirth, and postpartum processes. During labor, oxytocin is released into the bloodstream in response to the stretching of the cervix and uterus, as well as nipple stimulation during breastfeeding. These actions facilitate childbirth, maternal bonding, and milk production. The hormone was first discovered by Henry Dale in 1906, and its molecular structure was determined in 1952. Oxytocin is also used clinically to induce labor. Estrogen has been shown to increase oxytocin secretion and enhance the expression of its receptor, the oxytocin receptor, in the brain. A single dose of estradiol in women can elevate circulating oxytocin levels. Oxytocin is synthesized as an inactive precursor protein encoded by the OXT gene. This precursor includes neurophysin I, a carrier protein for oxytocin. The precursor undergoes enzymatic hydrolysis to release the active oxytocin nonapeptide, a process catalyzed by peptidylglycine alpha-amidating monooxygenase (PAM). The activity of PAM depends on vitamin C (ascorbate), which acts as a cofactor. Interestingly, sodium ascorbate has been found to stimulate oxytocin production in ovarian tissue in a dose-dependent manner. Tissues such as the ovaries, testes, eyes, adrenals, placenta, thymus, and pancreas, which contain PAM, also store high concentrations of vitamin C. Oxytocin is metabolized by oxytocinase enzymes, including leucyl/cystinyl aminopeptidase, and its degradation can be inhibited by compounds like amastatin, bestatin, leupeptin, and puromycin. In the hypothalamus, oxytocin is produced by magnocellular neurosecretory cells in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei. It is stored in Herring bodies at the axon terminals in the posterior pituitary and released into the bloodstream from the neurohypophysis. These axons also project to other brain regions, such as the nucleus accumbens, where oxytocin receptors are expressed. Oxytocin's endocrine effects and its cognitive or behavioral effects are thought to be coordinated through these projections. Additionally, oxytocin is produced by neurons in the paraventricular nucleus that project to other brain areas and the spinal cord. Depending on the species, oxytocin receptor-expressing cells are found in regions like the amygdala and the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis. In the pituitary gland, oxytocin is packaged in dense-core vesicles bound to neurophysin I, a peptide fragment derived from the oxytocin precursor. Its secretion is regulated by the electrical activity of oxytocin-producing cells in the hypothalamus. These cells generate action potentials that propagate down axons to nerve endings in the pituitary, where oxytocin-containing vesicles are released via exocytosis upon depolarization. Oxytocin concentrations in the brain can be up to 1,000 times higher than peripheral levels. Outside the brain, oxytocin-producing cells have been identified in tissues such as the corpus luteum and placenta in females, Leydig cells in the testes in males, and the retina, adrenal medulla, thymus, and pancreas in both sexes. The presence of oxytocin in these tissues raises questions about its potential roles beyond the central nervous system. In males, Leydig cells in some species, such as rats and guinea pigs, possess the machinery to synthesize oxytocin de novo. In females, oxytocin is synthesized by the corpora lutea in species like ruminants and primates. Along with estrogen, it induces the endometrial synthesis of prostaglandin F2α, which causes regression of the corpus luteum. Oxytocin-like nonapeptide hormones are found in virtually all vertebrates, supporting reproductive functions, while vasopressin-like nonapeptides are involved in water regulation. These two genes are typically located close to each other on the same chromosome and are believed to have arisen from a gene duplication event approximately 500 million years ago. Oxytocin exerts both peripheral (hormonal) and central (brain-mediated) effects through specific oxytocin receptors, which are G-protein-coupled receptors requiring magnesium and cholesterol. These receptors belong to the rhodopsin-type (class I) group of G-protein-coupled receptors. Oxytocin has been studied for its roles in behaviors such as orgasm, social recognition, pair bonding, anxiety, and maternal behaviors. Peripheral oxytocin actions primarily reflect secretion from the pituitary gland, while its behavioral effects are thought to result from release by centrally projecting oxytocin neurons. Oxytocin receptors are expressed in various brain and spinal cord regions, including the amygdala, ventromedial hypothalamus, septum, nucleus accumbens, and brainstem. In lactating mothers, oxytocin facilitates the milk ejection reflex by acting on the mammary glands. Suckling by an infant triggers spinal nerve signals to the hypothalamus, causing oxytocin neurons to fire action potentials in bursts, leading to pulsatile oxytocin secretion from the pituitary. Oxytocin also induces uterine contractions during labor and postpartum uterine involution. It may reduce urine excretion and, at high doses, cause hyponatremia. In rodents, oxytocin and its receptors are found in the heart, where they may play a role in embryonic heart development by promoting cardiomyocyte differentiation. Oxytocin modulates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, indirectly inhibiting the release of adrenocorticotropic hormone and cortisol under certain conditions. It also prepares fetal neurons for delivery by crossing the placenta and inducing a switch in the action of the neurotransmitter GABA from excitatory to inhibitory, silencing the fetal brain during delivery and reducing vulnerability to hypoxic damage. Oxytocin has been implicated in appetite regulation, with neurons in the paraventricular hypothalamus playing a key role in suppressing appetite. This population of neurons is absent in Prader-Willi syndrome, a genetic disorder characterized by uncontrollable feeding and obesity. Oxytocin has been linked to autism, with studies suggesting associations between autism and genomic deletions or aberrant methylation of the oxytocin receptor gene (OXTR). It also plays a role in social bonding, as seen in prairie voles, where oxytocin release during sexual activity facilitates pair bonding. In humans, oxytocin levels rise during positive social interactions, such as petting dogs or sharing food. Oxytocin increases trust and generosity, enhances empathy, and modulates social behaviors.
